entries.title: The Sensualist by Gary Shteyngart review – a delectable romp through life’s pleasures
entries.summary: From martinis to capybara videos, the novelist celebrates the little things (some more expensive than others) that bring him joyIn 2024, the novelist Gary Shteyngart flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. entries.content:
In 2024, the novelist Gary Shteyngart flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoe­maker Yohei Fukuda. A short king (“five foot five and a half, with that ‘half’ doing a lot of work”), Shteyngart dreamed of a fit to disappear his 52-year-old moobs (“my tatas”, “my chimichangas”) and melt the heart of the toughest maitre d’ at the most in-demand restaurants.

And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. Trying it on two days after Trump’s second election, “it was the final certificate of naturalization … I couldn’t make my adopted country fall out of love with fascism, but at least I could enjoy my new shoes.” Clothes become an advanced form of self-care.

In this first collection of essays, Shteyngart makes the case for pleasure in a world of joyless productivity. Screw Mark Zuckerberg in his monk’s hoodie. Screw the oligarchs and the mindful drinkers. Here’s a better life hack: choose two best friends “and form a martini trio for life”. Shteyngart adores chilled vodka, old watches and giant rodent TikTok. Again, this is self-care: “‘They regulate you down,’ my shrink told me … as we watched a video that featured superimposed capybaras sashaying down a fashion runway.”

When Shteyngart loves a thing, he is all in. His capybara odyssey takes him from Tokyo to Florida and on to South America, where he shadows a Brazilian capybara influencer and witnesses a standoff between marauding rodents and a swanky new development in Buenos Aires. Yes, they are weird and cute, with their “coconut-shaped” bodies and buck-teeth that never stop growing – but Shteyngart also feels they are the animal for the zeitgeist: “a desperately friendly creature always afraid of being attacked … Do we all feel trapped in a world that encourages us to be hyper-social yet rewards us with nothing but endless existential anxiety?”

He got into martinis for health reasons (less sugar than beer or wine) though this is easy to forget when Shteyngart is 10 drinks down on a New York bar crawl, trying to engage a wall mural in conversation. A martini is “the elixir of quietude”, he tells us, quoting EB White, though he prefers “friendship juice”. Friends are another revolt against the individualist new world order, and in an introduction Shteyngart mentions he has lost three close ones in the past five years. He doesn’t dwell on this; instead he takes Gerri from Succession (Shteyngart was a consultant on the TV show) to her favourite martini joint in the Village.

Fine suits, cuddly capys, cool celebrities: the world unfurls smoothly before Shteyngart, except in Brooklyn, where he is ignored by waiters while millennials down their fruits de mer. As befits a sensualist, his style is deeply pleasurable, great lolloping sentences meeting the punchline of a short one, the jokes generous and surprising. The tone is confiding, charming, often unreservedly silly. I have no idea why Shteyngart decides that wearing a T-shirt with the slogan DADDY’S LITTLE MEATBALL will be the perfect icebreaker on a cruise ship but he brilliantly milks it: “the very sight of me (small, ethnic, without a cap bearing the name of a football team) elicits no reaction from other passengers”.

Shteyngart teaches writing at Columbia and mentions that pleasure has been notably missing from his students’ work. Could it be that they can’t afford it? His sensualism is very expensive, a long way from touching grass, and the moral case for it retrofitted to a series of articles that tell us more about American magazine budgets than the national mood. Is getting a beautiful suit an act of rebellion or a tremendous treat? The Atlantic footed that bill, while the New Yorker picked up the capybara tab, and each essay to some degree reflects the ambition of the editor who commissioned it. The travelogues (for Travel + Leisure magazine) are the most narrowly observational; a parenting piece for Men’s Health is sweet but familiar.

The most outrageous, and least sensual, expense is the cruise, for which the Atlantic forks out $19,000 for a last-minute suite. The trip is predictably hellish, with its bad food, litter-strewn pools and Ayn Rand-spouting passengers, and even Shteyngart thinks the conceit (smart interloper infiltrates hoi polloi) has had its day. David Foster Wallace made it look easy in 1996, and it is. Docking at St Kitts, Shteyngart emails to ask if he can abandon ship. “‘It would be funny …,’ my editor replies. ‘Now get on the boat.’”

Being funny is the point, a pleasure in itself, but Shteyngart is at his best when his satire has more bite. A week in a Four Seasons hotel watching Russian state TV starts in dilettantish fashion, the author lolling on the bed with wagyu beef and pinot noir, but builds to something more sad and meaningful. “What a powerful weapon Putin’s television is,” he writes. “How skilfully it combines nostalgia, malice, paranoia … unless you’re a true believer, its endless din just reminds you of how alone you are in another man’s designs.”

Shteyngart’s own parents have become radicalised, as have his friends, a generation who rant “about the possibility of catching critical race theory from an open jar of mayonnaise”. Caught between the duelling propaganda of Fox News and Russian TV, they are fearful of vaccines and full of strange advice. His own is to find your personal bulwark of “immense, ecstatic, unencumbered ahistorical joy”. Hug a capybara, pour a drink, buy a $4,000 watch. Cheaper options are available.

entries.title: Michael by Bob Mortimer review – heartwarming quirkiness from the comedian
entries.summary: Mortimer’s off-kilter charm energises the story of a troubled teenager in 1970s MiddlesbroughIn comedian Bob Mortimer’s fourth novel, Michael, when we meet him, isn’t an angel; but he’s in a place that he suspects is at least angel-adjacent. entries.content:
In comedian Bob Mortimer’s fourth novel, Michael, when we meet him, isn’t an angel; but he’s in a place that he suspects is at least angel-adjacent. He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. He lands, somewhat trepidatiously, on the year he turned 14.

So back down memory lane we amble, the mysterious and otherworldly frame story intruding only in brief chapters now and again, recounting our hero’s comically tetchy exchanges with Charles. Here, really, is a sweet coming-of-age story with a delicate frosting of It’s a Wonderful Life.

We’re in Middlesbrough, 1978. Michael is weedy, an outsider at school, coping with the fallout from his alcoholic dad’s death and his loving mother’s new relationship with a boorish builder called Craig, who is marked as a wrongun from the start by his “curly brown hair, bushy sideburns, and pale grey eyes that were close enough together to give each other a kiss”. That, and the word “drywall” tattooed on his forearm.

Michael strikes up a tentative friendship with a schoolmate, Briony, and then with another school outsider – potential love triangle ahoy – but otherwise he prefers to retreat to his bedroom and draw. Craig, nevertheless, insists on taking him to the football, which he endures but doesn’t like much. A couple of Craig’s more genial mates give him some casual work clearing rubbish (Michael solemnly itemises the peculiar items they discover). And a neighbour, a kindly but disconcerting music teacher, takes Michael under his wing and becomes a sort of mentor to him.

The narrative unfolds in a string of comic episodes, and the period furniture is all there, lovingly detailed, just the right side – though only just – of those Instagram accounts called things like “Do You Remember Opal Fruits?”. (Actually, Mortimer is even more niche: we encounter at one point some Opal Mints. I don’t remember Opal Mints.) And why not? If David Mitchell can pay loving attention to Findus Crispy Pancakes in Black Swan Green, Bob Mortimer can do it for Opal Mints in Michael. Not to mention potato waffles, Birds Eye boil-in-the-bag beef, Ski yoghurt, Caramac, variety packs of Fox’s biscuits and ham sandwiches washed down with Lowcocks Dandelion and Burdock. And, yes, Findus Crispy Pancakes.

Mortimer’s huge charm as a comedian, and above all his gift for the slightly off-kilter phrase or the unexpected simile, is abundant in the text. I say “as a comedian” because there’s the case to be made that, especially in a first-person narrative, it’s more a comedian’s gift than a novelist’s. “She occupied a large round face with upturned nostrils that gave her the appearance of a werepig”: the word “occupied”, there, is very Bob Mortimer. Comparators include “like a crispy deceased mouse in an attic”, “like a friendly, confused walnut”, “like a lizard supping on a melted ice pop”, and of rain on a fibreglass roof, “like a thousand mice breaking in their new boots”.

But beneath the gags and the low-key surrealism there’s a pulse of real fear and sorrow. This is a touching story and it gets more so. Michael pushes down his grief for his father and his fears that his mother will take her own life, but they erupt here and there in passages that are more affecting for their contrast with the people-pleasing quirkiness that surrounds them. This is the story of a hurt boy, fundamentally a little scared of the world, wrestling with adult feelings and decisions he doesn’t feel ready to take. You may tend to resist descriptions like “heartwarming” and “life-affirming”, but that’s what Mortimer shoots for and that, in his amiable and original way, is what he hits.

entries.title: ‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her
entries.summary: A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look backPublisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New Y
entries.content:
Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes.

“But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”.

Highsmith, who was born in Fort Worth, Texas, in 1921, had a hit with her 1950 debut, Strangers on a Train, boosted by Alfred Hitchcock’s film. A perfect second novel, lesbian road trip The Price of Salt (later republished as Carol), sold a million copies under the pseudonym Claire Morgan, and The Talented Mr Ripley (1955) was a critical success. But around the mid-1960s, Highsmith’s American luck ran out: her agent wrote that her books were “too subtle”, her characters too unlikable, to make it into paperback. By 1984 she was without an American publisher.

“She never found a home because she was so unpleasant,” Penzler says. “I don’t think anybody said, ‘Oh look, we’re losing money but I love her so much, let’s keep her.’” Not yet knowing this, he signed a six-book deal with Highsmith, creating a new imprint in the process. “Pat didn’t want to be identified as a mystery writer, so I started Penzler Books.” He knew Highsmith’s first editor, Joan Kahn. “When I told her I’d bought Pat, she said: ‘God, what’s wrong with you?’ Later we agreed she was a monster.”

In Anton Corbijn’s new film A Talent for Murder, adapted from Joanna Murray-Smith’s 2014 play, Switzerland, a dying Highsmith is played by Helen Mirren, who nails her physicality with dark contact lenses, a wig and a way of seeming to make her neck disappear. By 1995, when the film is set, Highsmith had lived alone for years, ending her last relationship with the translator Monique Buffet, then 27, when she was 66. Tortured by her sexuality, unrequited love and a poisonous mother, happiness largely eluded her.

The film’s premise is that a young American editor must persuade Highsmith to write one last Ripley novel: if she signs, his job is guaranteed and her uncertain legacy assured. It’s a fiction, of course, though lovingly built on real details, from the water glasses filled with cigarettes to her tank of pet snails and the Bond villain bunker she designed.

The image of the misanthrope has helped keep Highsmith’s legacy alive, with Ripley recently remade by Netflix, but has the knife-collecting sadist become a caricature? Did she deserve greater recognition in America? She hated publicity, which made life tricky for her champions. Penzler remembers that on one book tour, “my wife and I took her to our most beloved Italian restaurant. A young publicist, whose job it was to take Pat to all the interviews, came with two long-stemmed roses. My wife said, ‘Oh, what a sweet thing!’ Pat threw hers on the floor without making eye contact. You can’t imagine a person like this.”

After that, Penzler took on chaperoning duties. The interviews were brief and sometimes never published. “The one time Pat said something positive was when I asked if she’d like to stop for a drink. She said, ‘I would have a beer. I like beer.’” Highsmith’s Swiss editor, Anna von Planta, recalled a similar first encounter in 1984: “Pat greeted me coolly, disregarding my extended hand. She then ordered a beer and fell silent.”

By 1967, Highsmith had begun a lifelong relationship with the Swiss publisher Diogenes, who took control of her literary estate when she died – as well as 56 volumes of unpublished diaries, letters and stories, neatly filed at the back of her linen cupboard. Those diaries laid bare Highsmith’s antisemitism and racism. In her introduction to a published edition of them, in 2021, Von Planta writes that Highsmith’s views have been represented faithfully, even where offensive, but that “in a handful of more extreme instances [we did] feel it our editorial duty to deny Pat a stage for them, in the same way we did while she was still alive”. Did Penzler ever feel she crossed a line? “She hated so much, including women. If there was antisemitism in her stories, I probably missed it because it was mild compared to the other things.”

Even those who were repelled by Highsmith’s prejudices shared an appreciation of her work – its strangeness, precision, gift for character and its unfashionable darkness. The horror of the Tom Ripley novels lies not so much in their violence (though there is plenty of that), as in his increasing enjoyment of it. Does he mean to murder an art collector with a bottle of Margaux in Ripley Under Ground? “Tom simply could not answer that. And did it matter, much?”, she writes. That bleakness sold better in Europe: even a weak late novel, Found in the Street, sold 40,000 copies in Germany compared with 4,000 in America.

Gary Fisketjon was Highsmith’s next and final American editor, at Atlantic and then Knopf. He died suddenly of a stroke on 7 November, aged 72, but when I spoke to him a week earlier he had nothing but good memories of her. She was no pussycat but nor were his other authors — among them Jay McInerney, Donna Tartt and Cormac McCarthy. He still had regrets over a lunch that never quite came together with Highsmith, Bret Easton Ellis and Michel Houellebecq, which would have been quite the nihilist triumvirate: you can draw a direct line from Tom Ripley to Patrick Bateman.

“We never had a cross word,” Fisketjon said on the phone from Oregon. “I took Pat for dinner at the Odeon, which was very popular. Kind of a chic, downtown, artistic crowd and whatnot, and she was just captivated. She was studying everybody in the room.” In a 1984 diary entry, Highsmith wrote that “it will be interesting to see what good writers come from the cocaine takers”, and in the mid-80s literary scene she had her answer.

At the Frankfurt book fair, she and Fisketjon talked about their cats. “She was a superstar in Germany, and she was careful to instruct me on the best way to drink their beer, with the foam on top.” Fisketjon published Found in the Street (1987) and the final Ripley novel, Ripley Under Water (1991), giving notes in the same way he would for anyone else. “The ideal was, and this happened a few times with Pat – she’d say, ‘I see what you’re getting at, but here’s a better way of improving it.’” When Hollywood scouts took him for lunch, he told them to look at Highsmith’s backlist. “But the notion of getting in touch with a Swiss publisher to make a deal was unusual. She was an outlier, living abroad.”

Fisketjon had passed on her final novel, Small g: A Summer Idyll, feeling he “couldn’t publish it as fervently as Pat deserved. She took it better than I feared.” They stayed friends, trading letters and cat news. He had seen A Talent for Murder a couple of days earlier, and liked it, while finding the plot implausible. “Dame Mirren’s expressions reminded me vividly of Pat, even if her personality was a lot darker than I ever saw.”

Liz Calder looked after Highsmith at Bloomsbury in the late 1980s until the author’s death, and gets a mention in her diaries: a dinner in Hampstead in 1992, with her “parrot called Jon-Jon – maybe 38, light green”. “Actually it was Juju,” Calder says, “but they communicated quite well. I think she was more interested in the parrot than any of us.”

Now 88, she remembers Highsmith as “very, very unusual. She would comment a lot on things around her – ‘look, something’s happening over there’ – or on what I was wearing. She was almost unsocialised.” At the same time, she had close friends in London, France and Switzerland. “People who were nothing to do with her work. She loosened up with me over time but I never met them.”

Highsmith died of lung cancer and anaemia on 4 February 1995, aged 74. The American papers ran obituaries but there was no bump in sales. When editor Robert Weil approached Diogenes about publishing a couple of her books at WW Norton in 1998, they insisted he acquire all 14 that were then out of print in America, including Strangers on a Train. “I was new at Norton. They said, ‘This is folly, the sales don’t bear up.’ But I was persistent.” He agreed to Diogenes’s terms, eventually taking on her last unpublished novel, Small g, as well as the Ripleys, Carol and dozens of unpublished stories.

Now an executive editor at the Norton imprint Liveright, Weil speaks from a New York office lined with Highsmith box sets. Actor Alden Ehrenreich spent time here while researching A Talent for Murder (“he was a wonderful fly on the wall”) and Weil thinks there is still more to be done with Highsmith. Small g was “not her best work”, but a new collection of short stories got “thundering reviews” in 2001. By then, Anthony Minghella’s 1999 film adaptation of The Talented Mr Ripley had renewed interest in her writing.

“What she could do in 12 pages was amazing,” says Weil. “Highsmith can write these stories where you feel stabbed at the end – she knows how to finish something.” He reckons there are at least five potential screenplays in a 2002 collection, Nothing That Meets the Eye, which must include A Girl Like Phyl, about a man who meets his lost love’s daughter on a plane (“The girl looked at him, happened to lift her eyes straight toward him, and Jeff felt as if he had been shot”) and the title story, about a woman who bewitches every man in a ski resort before jumping from a mountain. Highsmith follows the body all the way down, to the “dark and final click” of death.

“There are a few happy stories,” Weil adds. “There’s an evocation of New York in the late 40s which is so precise and loving. But she had a gimlet eye for hypocrisy.” Exile gave her clarity. “She learned to skin and savage America. She never left it psychologically.” In her understanding of greed, she is like Edith Wharton, Weil says. “But in terms of psychological manipulation, there are very few like Highsmith. She was so far from the mainstream, and she should have been a debutante from Dallas.”

Highsmith was rude and sometimes bigoted. She also had a capacity for friendship, and for work that would have been impossible without empathy. Both things can be true, as her favourite creation Ripley attests – beneath the good man lies an evil one; beneath her cruel exterior lay someone capable of kindness.

In March 1995 Liz Calder caught a train to Highsmith’s memorial service at the Chiesa di Tegna in Switzerland, accompanied by her UK agent Tanja Howarth. They had both found Highsmith difficult. “But we wanted to go. And it was very strange – it was well attended but not by many publishing people. Tanja and I didn’t know anybody.” The Highsmith they knew was not the one her friends mourned. She was a mystery to the last.

entries.title: The unexpected power of fleeting friendships
entries.summary: From Aristotle on, we’ve learned to see long-lasting relationships as more valuable. But what does that leave out?In Russian, a poputchik is a stranger you meet on a journey who you end up confessing everything to because you know you’ll never see them again. Like the English “fellow traveller”, poputchik was repurposed to describe Marxist sympathisers, but the original meaning intrigues me most.T
entries.content:
In Russian, a poputchik is a stranger you meet on a journey who you end up confessing everything to because you know you’ll never see them again. Like the English “fellow traveller”, poputchik was repurposed to describe Marxist sympathisers, but the original meaning intrigues me most.

The idea that we might safely unburden ourselves to strangers, or have their secrets bestowed upon us, is deeply embedded in Russian culture. It’s there in Leo Tolstoy’s The Kreutzer Sonata: as the windows tremble and the tundra passes in a hypnotic blur, Pozdnyshev tells his life story of marriage, betrayal and murder. Or in Venedikt Erofeev’s 1970s satire Moscow to the End of the Line, in which a retired cable fitter drunkenly hops a train and unfurls a sublime monologue on politics, society, love and, of course, vodka. A Russian friend jokes that this is “therapy, Soviet-style”.

Despite the fact that the proliferation of headphones and devices makes talking to strangers seem almost radical, most of us can probably tell our own poputchik tale. Perhaps we exchanged intimate secrets with someone on a car-share ride, or in an airport bar, or on that holiday when the coach broke down.

Earlier this year, on a long-haul flight to Toronto for work, I was seated among a group of excited young lads. My heart sank (though, for the record, they were impeccably behaved). Theirs must have too, finding a flustered, middle-aged bespectacled type in their row, instead of a pretty young thing to flirt with. We headphoned up and politely ignored each other, until at 4am, everyone gently snoring around us, my neighbour and I got to whispering. It turned out they were a group of Royal Navy submariners undergoing training off the icy Canadian coast.

Naturally I was dying to know all the details of their underwater life, but what I really remember was his shy admissions that he longed for a girlfriend – with months spent away it was hard to make a connection – and his worries about the talk he was due to give. In turn, I confided my fears around a recent career change. Then the lights pinged on, the cabin stirred and shifted, and we melted back into our separate worlds, wishing each other good luck when we disembarked. It was a disarming and expansive moment of shared vulnerability.

In our lonely and divided times, these fleeting intimacies with strangers are vital, though we’ve long been taught to dismiss them. Writing in the fourth century BC, Aristotle created a hierarchy of friendships that still haunts us today. At the top was the “perfect friendship”, a lifetime meeting-of-minds. At the bottom were a rag tag of convenient, pragmatic alliances, struck up to pass the time or for mutual assistance.

What made these lesser friendships unworthy was that they seemed disposable: “when the motive of the friendship is dissolved, the friendship is done away with,” Aristotle wrote with a disapproving sniff. It might be a stretch to describe someone I’d spoken to for an hour a friend, but if Aristotle was right, and the length of a relationship is the measure of its value, then fleeting connections ought to be the least worthy of our attention or interest.

Yet most of us recognise these connections can touch us in profound and lasting ways. Instead of Aristotelian hierarchies, perhaps it’s time to embrace the concept of “relationship anarchy”, which circulates in polyamorous communities. Relationship anarchists argue against ranking our romantic relationships, neighbours, long- and short-lived friendships, inviting us instead to see the singular value and qualities of each connection.

The evidence certainly suggests there are important benefits to even the most seemingly inconsequential connection with a stranger. Even small talk about, say, the weather can increase our sense of belonging and connection (it is more the form than the content that matters, researchers say). We frequently imagine that what distinguishes a close friend is that we can tell them anything, but just as often, we feel safe confiding in strangers, since they are less likely to judge or pepper us with intrusive follow-ups. In Shoji Morimoto’s 2023 memoir Rental Person Who Does Nothing, about his service offering company to strangers while they perform their chores, he observes: “There are a lot of important things that can be talked about with people you don’t know very well or even at all. Depth of discussion and depth of relationship don’t always go hand in hand.”

However sceptical we are of online spaces, and with good reason, they are one place we can exchange our secrets with strangers with relative ease. In the 1990s, trans people gathered in early internet chatrooms. Known only to each other by their handles, and often disappearing without warning, they forged temporary friendships that were nonetheless highly significant: in 1991, Terri Main, a 39-year-old trans woman, compared visiting CompuServe’s GenderLine forum to being enveloped in an “electronic hug”.

But while they can act as a lifeline, online encounters are different in important ways from real-world ones. So much in emotional connection happens unconsciously, a question of tone and rhythm, gesture, even smell. Real-world conversations also carry a different level of risk, since we can’t just log off when things go wrong, as they inevitably will (even Russian railway carriages had their fair share of opinionated bores, and other menaces). In the real world, we must learn to negotiate, to tolerate awkwardness and difficulty, to tactfully divert or withdraw. It is delicate, daring work, and its costs do not fall equally on all people. But if we neglect these social muscles entirely, they atrophy.

And there is so much to be gained, and to be learned. I don’t remember the name of the young man I met on the flight to Toronto. But I do remember exactly how the exchange made me feel. Connected and curious. Unburdened, Soviet-style. But most of all, awed by the extraordinary lives of others.

Tiffany Watt Smith is the author of Bad Friend (Faber). To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Further reading

Moscow to the End of the Line by Venedikt Erofeev (Northwestern University Press, £26.99)

Friends by Robin Dunbar (Little, Brown, £13.99)

Friendaholic by Elizabeth Day (4th Estate, £16.99)

entries.title: ‘It’s like the wild west’: how AI has rocked the literary world
entries.summary: With authors losing lucrative deals and writers removed from prize shortlists, accusations of AI use are sending shock waves through the publishing industry. Is it too late to turn the tide on machine writing?The romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn
entries.content:
The romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn to dark romance, a subgenre featuring twisted, toxic love stories that was taking off online but that publishers didn’t want to touch. Three years later, things were going well enough that she decided to self-publish full-time.

Kindle Unlimited, where Hart sells her books, rewards prolific writers: the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month. Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself “high six figures”.

Like any Kindle Unlimited author, she is only paid per pages read: it would make no business sense for her to churn out books that readers quickly abandon. “A bad writer or a bad storyteller is not going to get a good book out of AI. You still need to understand craft. You still need to understand structure. You still need to know what a reader wants,” she tells me, speaking via videocall from her home in South Africa. “So, it’s not taking the human out of the equation. It’s taking the friction and the time and the business blocks out of the way.”

One study (awaiting peer review), led by Tuhin Chakrabarty of Stony Brook University, estimates that around one fifth of recently self-published books contain at least 25% AI-generated text. Hart now teaches courses on how to use AI to produce books. Unless disclosing the use of AI becomes a legal requirement, she advises other authors not to do so because of the public response.

“The minute someone discloses [AI use] they get death threats, they get called names, they’re ousted,” she says. Hart is one of her pen names. After she talked to the New York Times earlier this year she was doxed and faced death threats. “I think the anger and hate comes from a place of fear,” she says. In the literary world, many people fear the tech will undercut and replace them. “I think people are very afraid of AI, and people in publishing are delusional in thinking that it’s not going to overtake our industry, that their screaming on social media is going to stop it.”

But the anger comes from another place, too. If large language models can spit out books that people want to read, or produce a convincing pastiche of your favourite writer, that’s almost certainly because they were trained on established writers’ stolen work. Last year, a class action lawsuit involving around 500,000 titles won a $1.5bn settlement from the AI firm Anthropic for alleged use of the writers’ work without consent. Other similar lawsuits are ongoing. Many writers oppose AI for both moral and aesthetic reasons. One group of 70 prominent authors wrote an open letter calling on the big five publishers – Penguin Random House, Hachette, HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster and Macmillan – to promise that they will “never release books that were created by a machine”. The publishers did not promise.

So where do we go from here? Will big name writers win the argument for keeping AI out of literature, or will our bookshelves and e-readers soon be crammed full of AI-generated stories? And if a reader can’t distinguish human from machine writing, does it still matter?

One literary agent told me that when it comes to AI, the atmosphere in mainstream publishing is like “the wild west”. The technology is outpacing the industry’s capacity to reckon with what it means that authors can – and already are – using AI to write their books. “We’re at a time where it’s all very much in flux, and I don’t think anyone has good answers – but certainly everyone’s talking about it,” says Liz Gately, a New York-based book scout.

Instead, there has been a spate of cancelled high-profile book deals and accusations against writers. In March, Hachette withdrew the romance novel Shy Girl from publication over evidence the author Mia Ballard used AI. Ballard claimed to the New York Times that an editor she hired may have been responsible for inserting AI-generated text. This year’s winner of the Commonwealth short story prize, Jamir Nazir, was accused of using AI, after readers – struck by odd phrases such as “she had the kind of walking that turned benches into men” – ran the story through Pangram, a leading AI detection program. He denies it. Pangram subsequently tested other entrants and concluded that since 2025, four regional winners were likely to have used AI.

In July, agents representing the debut novelist Jerry Falade withdrew from an eye-popping $2m (£1.5m) book deal after he was accused of using AI. He denied using AI for anything other than research. And then, last month, the Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien’s novel was struck off the Goncourt Academy longlist, France’s most prestigious literary prize, after social media users ran his novel through AI detection software. He, too, denied using AI to write his novel, but did admit to plagiarism in some of his other writing, including a short story he wrote more than a decade ago. After conducting its own investigation, his publishers Boréal dropped him in late October.

Falade – who like everyone I contacted in relation to these scandals declined to speak to me on record – wrote an essay pointing out that writing by non-native speakers or in “culturally unfamiliar” English is more often treated with suspicion. He also suggests the accusations against him may be tinged with racism. “I haven’t seen this kind of investigative zeal directed at white authors accused of using AI …” he writes, “apparently that level of scrutiny is reserved for a Black boy from Nigeria.”

It is true that every writer at the centre of these AI scandals has been an author of colour. In May, the author Steven Rosenbaum – who is white – was found to have accidentally inserted fabricated quotes into his book The Future of Truth: How AI Reshapes Reality when he used AI, which he disclosed in the acknowledgements. He said he regretted the errors but added that it “serves as a warning about the risks of AI-assisted research and verification”, which is why he wrote the book. His book wasn’t withdrawn.

One big problem is that when writers are accused, it is hard for them to clear their names. There is no definitive proof either way. Literary agents and book scouts are professional readers and say most AI-generated submissions (and these days they receive many) are very easy to spot. But, clearly, human judgment isn’t flawless, and evidence suggests that non-native and neurodivergent writers are more likely to raise false suspicion. Academic research estimates that Pangram is at least 95% accurate at detecting AI-generated writing, and it has near-0% rate of false positives – suggesting it is extremely unlikely that the tech would falsely label human-generated writing as AI.

Hannah Bowman, chair of the Association of American Literary Agents’ (AALA) AI special committee, says there’s disagreement on the way forward: some agents think AI detection software should be used routinely, others advocate for relying on relationships of trust. “I think it’s a shame that all of these things are getting addressed so publicly,” she says, with many scandals starting when journalists or social media users run work through AI detectors. “I worry for authors when they don’t have a chance to make a case in defence of their work … there needs to be a fair and thoughtful process, where if publishers and agents have concerns, they can discuss them with the authors.”

In the meantime, Gately, the book scout, says many agents have started recommending their writers don’t send documents as PDFs and save multiple drafts of their work (rather than resaving the same document) in case they are subject to AI accusations. The pervasive anxiety among agents and writers manifests in strange ways. One agent told me they were shocked to receive a manuscript from a writer they had worked with for many years – and who professed to hate AI – that used suspiciously “bizarre” words. She contacted the writer, who was “horrified”: the problem wasn’t that she’d used AI; it was that she was terrified of being accused of doing so and her efforts to make her prose sound “non-AI” had backfired badly.

Another unresolved question is if and when publishers should withdraw books. If Falade’s book was good enough to impress multiple publishers and attract an astonishingly high, multimillion-dollar advance, does it matter how it was written? (Falade, incidentally, has recently signed with a new agent.)

Thad McIlroy, a publishing expert and author of The AI Book Revolution, says he was surprised when Shy Girl was cancelled. The cancellation was partly his fault. After being alerted to online rumours that the book was written using AI, he decided to run it through Pangram, and then approached the New York Times. “I felt so stupid when [Hachette] cancelled it because it never occurred to me that that would have been the response,” he tells me. He anticipated that the publishers would either clean up the text or issue a disclosure on how AI was used. Shy Girl started out as a highly successful self-published novel, and the AI rumours started before Hachette acquired the manuscript. Once bought, the publishers edited the text considerably. McIlroy says he therefore finds it hard to believe that no one raised AI-concerns internally. Plus, he says, it’s a “really powerful book” that clearly resonated with readers, so why drop it the moment the story hit the media?

Both AI enthusiasts and haters say there’s an urgent need for more guidance from publishers, who hold the purse strings and are therefore the kingmakers in the books’ world. McIlroy says publishers need to be “brave” and publish extensive AI policies, outlining how they use the technology in-house and what authors are and aren’t allowed to do. He wonders if publishing houses aren’t doing this because they are in denial about AI, or if they are worried about alienating their highest-earning writers, who are almost all vehemently opposed to the tech. Tess Callero, a literary agent with Europa Content who describes the prospect of AI-generated fiction as “scary”, says she thinks publishers are biding their time because they want to keep the door open for AI. “If the big five publishers were coming down and saying we will not accept [AI-generated writing] it would be taken more seriously,” she says. “But they’re not, and you have to wonder the reason they aren’t. Is it because they see a future in which potentially these books could be monetised?”

One issue is US copyright law, which specifies that a book must be “human authored” and considers AI-generated text public domain. “Which is why it’s so problematic for publishers – because if it’s AI, they have no protection, they can’t have exclusive rights,” says Natalie Lakosil, a literary agent and chair of the copyright committee at the AALA. US copyright law protects AI-assisted work, but if the text has been produced by a machine it risks legal challenge (even if the copyright office, which asks for little detail, accepts the registration). It seems likely, Lakosil says, that this principle will be challenged in the courts eventually, but she is doubtful that the “human authored” requirement will be substantially changed. “The purpose of copyright protection is to protect human creation, to protect artists, and AI is not an artist,” she says. That said, she does believe the law needs to find ways to accommodate writers who want to experiment creatively with AI. She says publishing is in the midst of a “freakout period” comparable to the advent of e-books, which didn’t kill the market – as many feared – but did permanently change it.

In 2023, Stephen Marche wrote the crime novella, Death of an Author, using three AI programs – it is, to anyone’s knowledge, the first AI-novel to be reviewed by the New York Times. It could only be released as an audiobook, because of copyright concerns. Marche has been experimenting with AI in his fiction since the early 2020s. “Publishing has both become incredibly moralistic and at the same time it keeps getting rocked by these scandals,” he tells me. “The people like me who are very conscious about its use, and who both understand the technology and its limits and are not using it in a cheap way, in a cheating way, we’re totally excluded. But you know the scammers will find a way.” He says he would love to see an “experimental blossoming of creative forms” using AI, as is already happening in the art world.

The way forward, Marche says, is full transparency: there is a “very clear moral line” in labelling what is and isn’t AI generated, just as we currently distinguish between fiction and nonfiction. Even those who hate the idea of AI writing (myself included) might recognise that on rare occasions it can be powerful, precisely when it is not trying to pass as human. In Vauhini Vara’s moving essay Ghosts, for example, she uses generative AI to express things she cannot bring herself to write about her sister’s death. The piece is a conversation between a human and a machine that explores the expressive limits, and possibilities, of both kinds of language.

Most likely, AI-generated books will enter mainstream publishing in some form, and will introduce more slop into the market. But Marche points out that our culture is already awash with dull, derivative stuff. He recently went to see a Hollywood action movie that was so formulaic that although it was not made with AI it may as well have been. “There’s this garbage out there that’s worthless, some of it is AI generated, some of it’s human generated. You’re trying to make meaningful shit in this context and how do you do that? Some of it’s going to be made by people. Some of it with AI,” he says.

In France, a new prize – the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA – was launched last month for fiction writers who are working with AI. It seems probable that some AI-assisted books will be good enough that discerning readers cannot necessarily tell that a human has not written them. A recent study, also led by Chakrabarty of Stony Brook University and awaiting peer review, found that in blind experiments, when expert readers (students on leading MFA writing programmes) compared passages written by their MFA colleagues and those written by AI models trained on established writers, and then fine-tuned, they tended to prefer the AI generated text. Would they still prefer the texts if they knew they were AI? Maybe some people will be happy to read such books, although even the most beautiful AI-generated text is a Frankenstein monster, borrowed feelings and observations about the human condition stitched together by an algorithm that has no human qualities, no capacity to love or to feel. But probably many readers would choose human writing. Every agent I spoke to felt committed to protecting the human. “We’re in the human creativity business, not in the business of giving robots jobs,” says Doug Wallace, managing director at Andrew Nurnberg Associates International, a network of literary agencies. AI is “not going to be a big problem because we won’t let it become a big problem”.

But then again, as a writer of course I would want to conclude there. Right now, to write without the aid of a machine is to swim against a strong cultural tide. I’ve lost track of how many friends, in professions other than journalism, have looked at me with something close to pity when I tell them I would never use AI to write, not only because of my contractual obligations or the reputational risk but because I still think I can offer something better than a machine. And yet, machine-generated language keeps cropping up in the places you’d expect to offer the greatest resistance to slop: not just in book submissions but in leading newspapers and literary magazines. Among the many minor AI news stories to bubble up while I worked on this article? A piece in the Times Literary Supplement on AI and the crisis of the author, which was removed from the website because of – you guessed it – allegations it had been written with AI.

entries.title: Families clear homes of David Walliams books after sexual offence allegations
entries.summary: Parents take action while several independent bookshops say they had already stopped stocking his titlesIn Sarah’s house, David Walliams has been a bedtime staple for years. entries.content:
In Sarah’s house, David Walliams has been a bedtime staple for years. Her children, aged eight, six and four, have dressed up as his characters for World Book Day – they love the over-the-top, unusual names and illustrations.

Now, all the books are going. “I’ll probably take them away and replace them with other authors,” says Sarah, a mother in west London. “Sooner rather than later, so they don’t realise.” If any of her children ask why, she will tell them “that his choices aren’t great and that I think we should be reading other books”.

This week a joint Guardian and ITV News investigation alleged that the children’s author used his position to pursue young women and girls for sex, including girls as young as 15. Walliams denies the allegations. HarperCollins stopped publishing new Walliams books last December and dropped his entire backlist in September.

For many independent children’s booksellers, the news only confirmed a decision made long ago.

Helen Tamblyn-Saville, owner of Wonderland Bookshop in Retford, Nottinghamshire, stopped stocking him in 2020. “They didn’t fit the ethos and values of my shop,” she says. Walliams’s books “punched down”, she believes, citing what she sees as “themes of racism, misogyny and classism” in his writings.

In 2021, HarperCollins removed a story about a Chinese boy – Brian Wong, Who Was Never, Ever Wrong – from future editions of The World’s Worst Children after complaints that it relied on harmful racial stereotypes.

In 2025, Tamblyn-Saville turned down an invitation to an event with him. “It feels very much as if the golden goose had to be protected, despite the clear red flags.”

Griffin Books in Penarth, south Wales, dropped his books about 18 months ago over “the low quality of the writing and his frequent use of offensive stereotypes”.

The Chicken and Frog bookshop in Brentwood, Essex, has not stocked him for a decade. Urmi, owner of Pickled Pepper Books in north London, has a blunter opinion: “We heard [rumours] about David Walliams at least five years ago and at that point chose to not stock his books,” she says. She believes that “everyone in the industry knew … so anyone that’s only just taking books off the shelf is only interested in profit”.

Mainstream stores have moved quickly. The Works, a budget retailer, said it had removed all David Walliams titles from sale and TG Jones confirmed it no longer sold his books in store or online. Waterstones said it was talking to HarperCollins about returning “the small number of copies which remain in stock in a few of our shops”.

Families are clearing their shelves too. One parent walked past a neighbourhood book-swap box this week and found it stuffed full of Walliams titles. Another mother joked that she would be burning hers, saying Walliams was “a knock-off Roald Dahl anyway”. Sarah hasn’t decided what to do with hers: giving them to a charity shop just puts them “back into the system”.

Walliams’ sales have been falling sharply – but they have not disappeared. Retailers sold 7,497 Walliams books over the past four weeks, worth £48,400, according to NielsenIQ BookData figures reported by The Bookseller.

In the same period last year, when he had a new book out, Walliams sold 102,000. Even so, almost 108,000 copies of his books have been sold so far this year, worth more than £702,000, and his titles have made more than £153m since 2008.

Public libraries are also facing a difficult decision. “This is a very sensitive issue involving deeply disturbing allegations, and some people may find the continued presence of these books upsetting,” said Isobel Hunter, CEO of the charity Libraries Connected.

“But we also have a long-established legal principle within the sector that all books should be available to the public unless the content itself is unlawful.

“So most library services have said that the books will remain in their collections until they are naturally weeded out and withdrawn under existing stock policy. That doesn’t mean, of course, that libraries are obliged to promote them or have them on display.”

Anecdotally, she said, demand had “dropped significantly in recent years”.

Some schools appear to be taking a harder line – several teachers told the Guardian they were removing Walliams books from their classroom shelves.

For Sarah, the principle is simple: “Kids need to understand that actions have consequences. If something’s not right, then we need to act upon it.”

entries.title: The best books to read in November and December: new paperbacks from Benjamin Myers, Jeanette Winterson and John Updike
entries.summary: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some must-read new paperbacks, from an experimental novel about a German actor to a study of how the arts can boost our health*** Continue reading...
entries.content:
Fiction

Fiction

Jesus Christ Kinski

Benjamin Myers

The German actor Klaus Kinski is known best for his testy collaboration with Werner Herzog, whose 1982 film Fitzcarraldo put Kinski in the title role, lugging a steamship over the Andes.

Benjamin Myers’s new novel plunges us into Kinski’s fevered mind during one of his last performances, a recorded solo stage show in West Berlin in 1971, where he delivered a ferocious monologue as Jesus. Showcased in a documentary released in 2008 by Peter Geyer, the act descended into chaos, Kinski arguing with hecklers before ending his monologue in a near-empty auditorium.

The book melds Kinski’s on-the-record words with imagined second-person recollection about, among other things, his capture by allied forces as a German conscript, a spell in a psychiatric clinic, and his innumerable sexual conquests.

Cut half a century later to West Yorkshire during lockdown, where an unnamed writer decides to write a book “about the dead German actor Klaus Kinski”. The project looks unsaleable from the off, not least because Kinski’s eldest daughter, Pola, accused him of sexually abusing her. There’s also the fact that “the writer” – let’s call him Benjamin Myers – owes his publisher a “long, era-spanning historical novel concerning an English saint”, and has already spent the advance (this is a reference to 2023’s Goldsmiths prize-winning Cuddy). Yet the “dark and forceful energy” of Kinski’s Jesus keeps drawing him back to online footage. By the time Myers clocks that the actor was 45 in 1971 – the age Myers is in 2021 – “a psychic door of communication [is] opened by the key of coincidence”, and it would basically be rude not to write the book.

This fitfully engaging narrative experiment isn’t really about Kinski or even Myers so much as the 21st-century cultural marketplace. As lapel-grabbing rants give way to downbeat musings, the book exerts a strange charm, ushering us behind the scenes of its own making. “I live freely,” Kinski boasts, unlike people “stuck in … dismal jobs”. Amid the keynote disaffection, you ultimately sense contentment, even joy, that he’s not the only one able to say so. Anthony Cummins

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

The True True Story of Raja the Gullible (and His Mother)

Rabih Alameddine

Meet Raja, the narrator of Rabih Alameddine’s new novel. A 63-year-old gay philosophy teacher and drag entertainer, he is a stickler for rules and boundaries, living in a tiny Beirut flat with his octogenarian mother, the nosy and unfettered Zalfa. Invited to a writing residency in the US, Raja will use the occasion to relate his life.

Winner of the 2025 US National Book Award for fiction, Alameddine’s seventh novel opens and closes in 2023, but the bulk of its action takes place earlier: encompassing the lead-up to and aftermath of the Lebanese civil war (1975-1990), the Covid pandemic, Lebanon’s 2019 banking crisis, and the Beirut port explosion in 2020. If this timeline makes the book sound like a punishing tour of Lebanese history, I promise it isn’t. More than a war chronicle or national exposé, it is a queer coming-of-age tale, an exploration of the bond between a mother and a son, and a meditation on storytelling, memory, survival and what it means to be truly free. Told in a voice as irresistibly buoyant as it is unapologetically camp, this rule-breaking spin on the trauma plot holds on to its cheer in the face of sobering material. Poignant but never cynical, often dark but never dour, wise without being showy and always eager to crack a joke, this is a novel that insists that the pain of the past need overwhelm neither present nor narrative, identity nor personality. With Sartre as his guide, and a drag fabulousness all his own, Raja shows us how. Yagnishsing Dawoor

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Crime and thriller

Crime and thriller

A Bad, Bad Place

Frances Crawford

Set in the late 1970s in the Possilpark district of Glasgow, an area riven by poverty, crime and sectarianism, Crawford’s superb debut is told from two points of view: 12-year-old Janey, who is walking her dog when she stumbles upon the body of a young woman; and her grandmother Maggie, who has cared for Janey since she was rescued, as a baby, from the gas explosion that killed her immediate family. Janey is afraid to tell the police all she knows, but finds herself caught up in the machinations of the grownup world. Maggie, who has secrets of her own, is desperate to protect her granddaughter, but poverty and lack of choice make her vulnerable, and the dead woman has connections to a well-known criminal family. A well-observed, well-told account of trauma, grief and the concomitant magical thinking, this coming-of-age mystery has flashes of humour and pathos that provide fuel for real suspense. Laura Wilson

£8.99 – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Crime and thriller

The Madman

Henning Mankell, translated by George Goulding and Sarah de Senarclens

Written in the 1970s and published in English for the first time, The Madman is set in a Swedish town in the late 1940s. The country’s wartime neutrality-on-paper continues to divide: the town’s pro-Nazis want the past forgotten, but the communist sympathisers, bitter about having been interned, want a reckoning. When a letter to this effect appears in the local paper, those accused, including the director of the town’s sawmill, claim that newcomer Bertil Kras has been stirring resentment for political ends. When the sawmill burns down, Kras is blamed for that, too, and the disintegration of the life he has tried to make provokes an existential crisis. An older Mankell might have been more concise, but the slow build towards inevitable disaster makes for true emotional depth, and the theme of othering, isolating and penalising people for their opinions remains horribly topical. Laura Wilson

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Letters

Letters

John Updike: A Life in Letters



John Updike had the mind of a middling middle-class postwar American male, and the prose style of a literary genius. Such a lord of language was he that even the notoriously grudging Vladimir Nabokov afforded him a meed of praise. A reviewer, musing on the disproportion between the style and content of Updike’s fiction, likened him to a lobster with one hugely overgrown claw. It was a comparison Updike was to remember – for all his bland urbanity, on display from start to finish in this mighty volume of his letters, he could be prickly, and did not take slights lightly.

At the heart of this volume we find the correspondence, from the first half of the 1970s, surrounding Updike’s separation and divorce from Mary, and his affair with and marriage to Martha – the biblical resonances of the names are almost too pat. These pages make for painful reading: Updike could be cruel – to Martha: “Mary’s body (her breasts!) would delight me still, if I could dissociate it from her pinched Unitarian soul …” – but in the main they are either pained, with Mary, or passionate, with Martha. And simultaneously, of course, he was having it off with other loves, old and new.

Are his books read now? Towards the end he made a glum self-assessment: “I have fallen to the status of an elderly duffer whose tales of suburban American sex are hopelessly yawnworthy period pieces.” Perhaps so; but he wrote such prose as to make the envious seraphim sigh. John Banville

£15.29 (RRP £16.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Science

Science

Art Cure

Daisy Fancourt

A professor of psychobiology and epidemiology at University College London, Fancourt researches how social connections and behaviours affect our health. In Art Cure, her first book for a popular audience, she aims to make a scientific case that the arts – from playing music to theatre-going to painting – aren’t a merely aesthetic aspect of life. Instead, they are deeply entwined with our mental and physical wellbeing at every level – from the workings of our cells and molecules to cognition, memory and mood. In an era of shrinking arts funding and overstretched healthcare systems, her message is urgent. But how to compile rigorous evidence for something as holistic, indefinable – and, perhaps, resolutely unscientific – as art?

Fancourt’s answer is to dissect artistic interventions and practices into their component parts. She argues that every arts experience can be broken down into “active ingredients”; could even – if we had the processing power – be converted into binary code. Singing to sick babies becomes a mix of noise buffering, neurological stimulation, human contact and stress reduction. These ingredients trigger biological mechanisms that lead to health outcomes, she explains, and we can test, refine and prescribe them just as we might any cocktail of drugs. With this approach in mind, she surveys the evidence for medical benefits, from wellbeing to brain health, chronic pain and even how long we live.

Art Cure cannot provide answers. But it does make a compelling, compassionate case for broadening how we think about medicine – to encompass people and communities, not just physical bodies, and to recognise that creativity, identity and purpose shape our biology as much as any drug. Jo Marchant

£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

History

History

Stay Alive: Berlin 1939-45

Ian Buruma

Berlin had always been a case apart. The legacy of the wild Weimar years – all that artistic and political radicalism, not to mention louche living – had continued under the Third Reich. The city remained defiantly itself and, despite the efforts of high command, mulish about being told what to do. That, at least, had been the situation in 1941.

By the time Ian Buruma’s father, a conscripted labourer from the Netherlands, arrived two years later, Berlin had begun grudgingly to toe the line. The war was going badly now, with the Russians pushing in from the east, and American and British bombs dropping from the skies. Food was scarce, Jewish citizens were being disappeared daily and Hitler and Goebbels, both frequently in the city, were getting more anxious and crueller by the day. Now whenever Berliners met each other in a food queue or a bomb shelter their most likely greeting was Bleiben sie übrig – “Stay alive”.

Nonetheless, argues Buruma, wherever you looked you could still find pockets of resistance. He isn’t referring here to well organised underground networks, but rather to ordinary men and women, not especially brave but still capable of doing the right thing. When Jews were ordered to start wearing identifying insignia, plenty of their fellow Berliners made a point of going up to them in the street and shaking hands. Young Leo Buruma, drafted in to work at a heavy engineering factory, took up with a Ukrainian girlfriend, pointedly ignoring the Nazis’ dictum that, as a “Germanic” Dutchman, he had no business consorting with an “inferior race”.

Other witnesses, such as journalists Ursula von Kardorff and Ruth Andreas-Friedrich, were careful to keep only scrappy and coded memos during the war, but subsequently reconstructed these into coherent narratives for publication. Von Kardorff could never be described as a resister, yet her memoir shows someone trying hard to remain decent in a criminal state. Her father, a successful portrait painter, had lost his teaching job thanks to his opposition to the regime, yet her mother, a textile designer, continued to kit out the homes of the Nazi grandees. Ursula herself delivers warm clothes to Jewish homes but wonders if she is merely doing it to salve her conscience. Her real anguish is reserved for her brother who is fighting for Germany on the eastern front.

None of this is morally coherent and yet, suggests Buruma in this wonderfully nuanced book, it was necessary if you wanted to stay alive, and knew yourself to be neither brave nor craven – but somewhere in the muddled in-between. Kathryn Hughes

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Memoir

The Uncool

Cameron Crowe

Crowe previously fictionalised his story in the 2000 film Almost Famous, which he wrote and directed. His lyrical and compulsively readable memoir The Uncool is bookended by the opening of a musical version, which coincides with the death of Crowe’s mother Alice whose aphorisms, including “Put some goodness in the world before it blows up”, are scattered throughout the book.

Crowe’s is a world of aftershow parties filled with characters like Freddie Sessler, a drug dealer who is rumoured to have made his fortune manufacturing pencils; late-night dressing-room jam sessions (Crowe has his guitar gently removed from his hands by a roadie called Red Dog when he attempts to join in with the Allman Brothers); eager, undamaged groupies (he knows a crew called the Flying Garter Girls whose leader Pennie Lane’s credo is “only blowjobs, and that’s it”); and, as the early 70s wear on, omnipresent cocaine use, though Crowe doesn’t partake. “I couldn’t shake the image of my teacher-mother popping up,” he says. “You’re killing brain cells!”

He shadowed Bowie at parties with Ronnie Wood and in the studio with Iggy Pop; he hung out with him day and night in houses he was renting, meaning that he was there to record the heartstopping moment when Bowie suddenly jumped to his feet mid-interview because he thought he’d seen a body fall from the sky.

The Uncool captures an extraordinarily inventive period in which rock music was stretching out in all directions, whether towards country music thanks to artists like Gram Parsons, or the conceptual in albums by the likes of Yes and the Who. Crowe was part of a burgeoning music press that, as well as recommending new bands to its readers, or conveying what rock groups had to say for themselves, would interpret, celebrate and contextualise the huge creative strides some of these musicians were making. Alex Needham

£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Joyride

Susan Orlean

Over the course of four decades, seven books and countless exquisite magazine features, especially for the New Yorker, Orlean has profiled celebrities and nobodies, followed cults and choirs, turned her eye to supermarkets and surfers. “Writers fall into two categories: there are those who have something they want to say to the world, and there are those who believe the world has something to tell them,” she observes. Orlean falls squarely into the second camp. There are two kinds of story she likes best: “hiding in plain sight” and “who knew?”.

A memoir is usually neither of these sorts of stories, but Orlean rises to the challenge of writing about her own life with grace. Joyride represents the liner notes to a career of hits. There’s the deliciously “heady, fun, surreal” experience of watching Spike Jonze’s movie Adaptation, based on her book The Orchid Thief, come to life – including being played by Meryl Streep. (Orlean’s account of flipping open Charlie Kaufman’s script for the first time to discover herself in it is laugh-out-loud funny.) A memorable Twitter thread from 2020 – the result of too much rosé on an empty stomach – that made her the “patron saint of pandemic drinking”, gets its moment, too. And harder episodes: a divorce, a cancer diagnosis, the sorrow of moving her mother into a nursing home.

Orlean sees the writing life as one of constant highwire creative reinvention – “you never build equity”, is how she puts it. Her father, who wanted to be writer but became a businessman instead, might have agreed: after she published The Orchid Thief he suggested she consider finally enrolling in law school. Thank goodness she didn’t. “I felt called, I really did, to describe ordinary life in a way that revealed its complexity and poetry – to show how rewarding it is to be open to and curious about the world, and how much joy can be found in letting yourself be surprised.” Mythili Rao

Essays

One Aladdin Two Lamps

Jeanette Winterson

In the framing device that opens the Middle Eastern folk tales collected in One Thousand and One Nights, King Shahryar avenges his wife’s infidelity by ordering her execution and marrying a new virgin every night, having each of them beheaded by sunrise so they won’t have time to cheat. When he runs out of victims, the young Persian queen Shahrazad volunteers but stalls her own murder by telling the king one captivating tale after another – and those become the stories we’re reading.

As Jeanette Winterson puts it in her new book – a dizzying whirligig of memoir, history, philosophy, politics and self-help, loosely tied to commentary on the Nights – Shahrazad’s feat of creativity “refuses the present emergency – the contrived drama of a powerful man”. The echo of life in the Trump era is deliberate; for Winterson, the means by which Shahrazad changes her predicament holds out hope for a progressive politics currently losing ground to “radical-rightwing thuggery”. “A better story starts with a better story,” she writes. “Reason will not win the day. Without imagination nothing changes.”

Each chapter opens with a pithy retelling of one of Shahrazad’s tales, spritzed with 21st-century idiom (“The Vizier … has no manosphere where he can vent”), before giving way to wide-ranging reflections on anything and everything, from the history of eugenics, to 13th-century Mali, to the awfulness of the trouser suits “preferred by some CEO types and lots of female politicians”. As opinions on matters big and small fly past, the tone evokes by turns a party political broadcast, Radio 4’s Thought for the Day, an old friend setting the world to rights. Anthony Cummins

Biography

Biography

The Curious Case of Mike Lynch

Katie Prescott

At least two terrible ironies surround the death of Mike Lynch. One lies in the name of his superyacht, which sank off the coast of Sicily in the early hours of 19 August 2024. He had named the boat Bayesian to honour Bayes’s theorem, a mathematical rule that helps you weigh up the probability of something given the available evidence, which served as Lynch’s guiding light over the course of a tempestuous career. The theorem was “a beautiful key to our minds”, Lynch believed. But it was entirely incapable of predicting the outcome that morning, when the yacht capsized during a storm, killing seven people, including Lynch, his 18-year-old daughter Hannah and his US lawyer, Chris Morvillo.

A second irony lies in the fact that Lynch had just come through the trial of his life, one he felt was bound to end in jail, where he thought he could die. Somehow, to everyone’s astonishment, an American jury had acquitted him and his co-defendant on all 15 counts of fraud.

To celebrate their win, Mike and his wife, Angela, decided to take the Bayesian on a series of cruises around southern Italy, inviting various supporters and associates. Lynch was no sailor, but he loved the seclusion the boat offered, and was immensely proud of its a 72-metre mast, one of the tallest in the world – a feature that some have speculated made it more vulnerable in strong winds, although the yacht’s manufacturer has defended its design. Through July and into August, it pottered around Capri and the Aeolian Islands. Then, in the middle of the month, the court victors were overtaken by a sequence of near-impossible coincidences, as Prescott sets out in pacily written detail. Charlie English

Politics

Politics

The Mission

Tim Weiner

Why has an organisation with huge amounts of money at its disposal, a record of recruiting the brightest and the best, and the widest of remits, failed to notch up a better record? It’s true that we may not know about many of the CIA’s successes. But we know about a lot of its failures, and some of them have marked US history ineradicably.

In The Mission, Tim Weiner, whose reporting on the CIA in the New York Times was always essential reading, and whose subsequent books on the US intelligence community have a place on the shelves of anyone interested in international affairs, provides a variety of answers to this essential question. As he showed nearly 20 years ago in Legacy of Ashes, his history of the CIA from its founding in 1947 to the end of the 20th century, the agency’s position by the end of the 90s was pretty desperate. It was starved of cash and bleeding talent. A high-flyer who had been station chief in Bucharest was revealed to be working for the Russians, handing them the names of large numbers of agents and employees. But the new US administration that came in at the start of 2001 wasn’t too worried. In March that year, Donald Rumsfeld, the defence secretary, told the joint chiefs of staff: “For the first time in decades, the country faces no strategic challenge.” Six months later came 9/11. The CIA had tried to convince the feckless George W Bush about the looming threat of Islamic ultra-fundamentalism, but no one in the administration listened. The agency was regarded as broken.

Weiner’s sources encompass several senior CIA figures from the period under discussion. These people opened up to him, and as a result the book contains many essential new details. Weiner’s account of Donald Trump’s links to Vladimir Putin in 2016 is clearly based on information from inside the agency, and it leads him to assert openly that Trump was Putin’s polezny idiot – his useful idiot. There are all sorts of other important and fascinating revelations in The Mission. No one has opened up the CIA to us like Weiner has. John Simpson
